profile.summary: The Gospel of John was written to produce faith in Jesus Christ, the Son of God, showing him closely as the revealer of the Father and the donor of eternal life. The book unites intimacy and depth: it presents memorable signs, discourses and encounters that lead the reader to recognize who Jesus is. In the context of Christians in Ephesus and in the midst of tensions with the Jewish environment and internal controversies, John offers a pastoral and apologetic witness, calling the church to believe, remain and witness. The authorship is traditionally linked to the apostle John, the beloved "disciple." the gospel itself does not explicitly declare it; the date is commonly situated around 90 AD, but this is also treated cautiously because it depends on tradition and historical inferences.
profile.setting: The setting involves the Christian community of Ephesus in Asia Minor at the end of the first century. These Christians lived between Jewish and Greek cultures, dialogue with local synagogues and facing debates about the identity of Jesus, their relationship with Abraham and the validity of the Christian faith. The gospel reflects close knowledge of Palestine, Jewish feasts and traditions of Jesus" time, but also explains some terms and references to readers who were no longer fully immersed in this world.

structure.label: Prologue and first signs
structure.description: It presents the entry of the Word into the world, the call of the first disciples and the episodes in which Jesus reveals himself through decisive signs and encounters, such as Cana, Nicodemos and the Samaritan woman.

structure.label: Jesus in the feasts and symbols of Israel
structure.description: It shows Jesus acting amidst Jewish feasts and reinterpreting signs and expectations of Israel, healing, feeding the crowd and revealing itself as fulfillment of what the old covenant pointed out.

structure.label: Lazarus, farewell and prayer
structure.description: Nar ra the resurrection of Lazarus, the last public call to the faith and then the farewell speech at the paschal dinner, in which Jesus prepares the disciples for his departure, promises the Spirit and prays for them.

structure.label: Passion, Resurrection and Commissioning
structure.description: Reports the arrest, interrogations, crucifixion and resurrection of Jesus, culminating in the apparitions to the disciples, in the granting of the Spirit and in the final instructions, including the restoration of Peter.

themes: Jesus as full revelation of the Father and the Son of God
Faith as a central response to apostolic witness
Light, life and victory of Christ over darkness and death
The action of the Holy Spirit in worship, in the new life and in mission
Unity between signs, cross, glory, and eternal life
readingKeys: Notice how the signs and discourses are not separated: the miracles reveal the identity of Jesus, and the speeches explain his meaning.
Note the recurrent contrast between faith and unbelief, especially in the reactions of characters such as Nicodemus, the Samaritan, Tomé and Pilate.
Read the final chapters as a continuation of the revelation of Christ's glory: the cross is not defeat, but a way to exaltation, mission and life.
profile.cautions: The introduction presented follows the traditional reading that associates the gospel with the apostle John, but indirectly recognizes that the text does not explicitly declare authorship; therefore, it is prudent to speak in traditional attribution and at an approximate date, not in absolute certainty. It is also appropriate to avoid imposing too much rigid division on the gospel, since its literary structure is woven by signs, discourses and conflicts that interpenetrate. This synthesis was elaborated only from the source provided, without resorting to additional external traditions.

dossier.narratedEra: The narrated time is the ministry, death, and resurrection of Jesus in the 1st century, in regions such as Galilee, Samaria, Judea, Bethany, Jerusalem and the Sea of Galilee, under Roman rule and amidst the Jewish leaderships of the period.
dossier.compositionEra: The composition is situated by the comments at the end of the 1st century AD, with strong association to Ephesus and the tradition of the Apostle John. Tyndale suggests conclusion around A.D. 90; Matthew Henry considers it more likely that the gospel was written before exile at Patmos, but recognizes the ancient tradition that places him in Ephesus and discusses other dates as after the destruction of Jerusalem.

politics.title: Roman dominion and the figure of Pilate
politics.detail: The gospel sets the passion of Jesus before the Roman governor Pontius Pilate. The notes place Pilate as governor of Judea of AD 2636 and place it in direct relationship with the high priest Caiaphas during a period of search for peace with Rome.
politics.readingImpact: Reading gains political weight: the death of Jesus is not only a religious conflict, but an event located under imperial surveillance and with potential for public repercussions.

politics.title: The Sanhedrin, Caiaphas and the calculation of public order
politics.detail: Caiaphas is presented as leader of the supreme council, afraid that the movement around Jesus provokes Roman intervention and destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple. The text highlights that his talk about "a man dying for the people" was ironic and politically pragmatic.
politics.readingImpact: This helps the reader realize that the rejection of Jesus was shaped by fear of national instability and imperial reaction, not just by theological dispute.

politics.title: Messianic expectations with political connotations
politics.detail: The notes claim that the Jews expected a Messiah who brought spiritual leadership and political redemption to Israel. They also note that Jesus" announcement as Messiah raised political implications that leaders judged dangerous.
politics.readingImpact: The reader understands why questions about Messianic identity in John sound explosive: confessing Jesus could be read as an affirmation of royal and national pretense.

politics.title: Conflict between Jewish and Christian communities
politics.detail: The introduction describes tensions between small Christian churches and local synagogues, with debates about whether Jesus was the Son of God, how could be the Messiah and whether Christians could claim to be Abraham's sons.
politics.readingImpact: This frame explains John's apologetic tone: the gospel is read as a response to real community controversies, not just as an abstract devotional narrative.

politics.title: The Threat of Persecution and Prudence of Jesus
politics.detail: In John 11 the notes reiterate that going to Jerusalem could mean death, that the region was politically tense and that Jesus made a prudent decision by withdrawing to Ephraim when the leaders began plotting his death.
politics.readingImpact: The movement of Jesus between Judea and the surrounding areas ceases to be mere geographical detail and becomes part of a strategy at real risk.

customs.title: Burial the same day and public mourning of seven days
customs.detail: The notes say that the dead were buried on the same day they died and that, in the case of Lazarus, the family and the residents maintained a public period of mourning of seven days, with loud mourning and collective lamentation.
customs.readingImpact: The miracle of John 11 becomes more vivid: the resurrection does not occur in a symbolic void, but in the face of funerary customs and intensely public mourning.

customs.title: Tombs carved in rock and closing stone
customs.detail: The tomb of Lazarus is described as a tomb excavated on the rocky hillside, with rolling stone at the entrance and inner chambers for burial.
customs.readingImpact: The order of Jesus to remove the stone highlights the physical reality of death and the concrete difficulty of the gesture, reinforcing the strength of the sign.

customs.title: Fishing as normal occupation of the disciples
customs.detail: In chapter 21, some disciples return to fishing in the Sea of Galilee, and the note clarifies that this does not indicate weakening of the faith; even rabbis kept their usual occupations.
customs.readingImpact: The reader should not interpret manual work as spiritual abandonment; John presents continuity between discipleship and daily work life.

customs.title: Food galilee of fish and bread
customs.detail: The meal prepared by Jesus on the beach is composed of fish and bread, described as basic elements of the galilee diet.
customs.readingImpact: The breakfast with the Risen One gains a domestic and everyday texture, underlining the body reality of the appearance.

customs.title: Purifications Jewish rituals associated with baptism
customs.detail: The notes of John 1 explain that Jewish baptisms were ritual washes for ceremonial purity after contact with impurity, and connect this with the requirement of confession of sins in the ministry of John the Baptist.
customs.readingImpact: The reader realizes that the theme of baptism in John dialogues with ritual practices known in Judaism, not with an isolated and abstract symbol.

customs.title: Servil position to take the sandal
customs.detail: Removing the sandal is presented as a task reserved for the slave, never to the disciple.
customs.readingImpact: When John the Baptist humbles himself before Jesus, the note highlights the social distance between servant and teacher and intensifies the exaltation of Christ.

language.title: Logos as a key opening
language.detail: The notes treat the prologue as an introduction to the 'logos' and claim that John uses the term to declare that Jesus is both God's revealing and God Himself. They also note that the term evoked, for Greeks, a rational principle of the universe, and for Jews, the word of the Lord and the creative wisdom of God.
language.readingImpact: This guides the reading of John 1 as a bridge between different cultural audiences, without reducing Jesus the mere philosophical idea or just a Jewish religious image.

language.title: Light and darkness as an image of revelation and conflict
language.detail: The prologue is read as an announcement of the light that enters the world and the hostility of darkness, which cannot extinguish or understand the light.
language.readingImpact: Helps to read the gospel as a narrative of revelation accompanied by increasing opposition, especially in the public ministry of Jesus.

language.title: Word/Tablenacle and the Divine Presence in Jesus
language.detail: The note associates the expression of John 1:14 by the verb 'arm his tent' and the tabernacle of the Old Testament, concluding that the glory seen earlier in the desert tent is now present in Jesus.
language.readingImpact: The symbolism of the tabernacle makes the reader see the incarnation as a concrete and cultual divine presence, and not only as a miraculous birth.

language.title: Amen double and solemnity formula
language.detail: In John, Jesus often introduces teachings with the duplicated Greek form am'n am'n, translated into the notes as a way of emphasizing the following speech.
language.readingImpact: The style reinforces the authority of Jesus" statements and draws attention to moments of decisive revelation.

language.title: I am and the divine identity of Jesus
language.detail: The notes highlight that John records Jesus using the language 'I Am', linked to the divine name of the Old Testament, as the affirmation of his divinity.
language.readingImpact: This strengthens the high Christological reading of the gospel: the statements of Jesus are not only self-affirmations, but revelations of his unique relationship with the Father.

language.title: "I am the resurrection and life" as central theological language
language.detail: In John 11, Jesus is presented as the one whose life is bound to victory over death, and the notes explain that the statement is not mere future promise, but a reality linked to communion with him.
language.readingImpact: The scene with Martha must be read as a revelation of who Jesus is, not just as pastoral consolation before the mourning.

timeline.title: Public ministry of Jesus structured in signs and speeches
timeline.detail: The notes divide the gospel into two great parts: chapters 1-12 as "Book of the Signs" and 13"21 as the Book of Glory." The first part covers the public manifestation of Jesus to the Jewish world.
timeline.readingImpact: This structure guides chronological and literary reading: signs are not loose episodes, but stages of growing revelation.

timeline.title: Rite and called initials around John the Baptist and the first disciples
timeline.detail: The narrative prologue places the testimony of John the Baptist, the encounter with the first disciples and the first recognitions of the identity of Jesus.
timeline.readingImpact: The beginning of the gospel is marked by progressive witness and adherence, not by an instantaneous and universal revelation.

timeline.title: Signs in Cana, Jerusalem, Samaria, and Galilee
timeline.detail: The notes summarize a sequence of events in which Jesus transforms water into wine, purifies the temple, dialogues with Nicodemus and finds the Samaritan woman, before other actions in Jewish feasts and signs in Galilee.
timeline.readingImpact: The reader perceives a geographical and theological expansion: Jesus reveals himself in Jewish contexts, Samaritans and festivals of the religious calendar.

timeline.title: Lazarus as a prelude to passion
timeline.detail: Lazarus' resurrection is presented as a foreshadowing of Jesus' death and resurrection; shortly afterward, Jesus is anointed for the burial and his hour of glorification begins.
timeline.readingImpact: John 11 is not only an isolated miracle, but the milestone that accelerates the narrative toward the cross.

timeline.title: Easter, Prison and Judgment
timeline.detail: After the paschal supper, Jesus crosses to Gethsemane, is imprisoned with the presence of Roman soldiers and temple guards, passes through interrogation of the Jewish council and is taken to Pilate for the crucifixion.
timeline.readingImpact: The paschal and judicial context shows passion as a liturgical, political and public event, not just as private martyrdom.

timeline.title: Resurrection, apparitions and final commission
timeline.detail: Chapter 20 describes the resurrection as climax and chapter 21 adds appearances in Galilee, Peter's restoration, and the reaffirmation of the call to follow Jesus.
timeline.readingImpact: The final reading of the gospel emphasizes testimony, mission, and discipleship continued after the resurrection.

investigation: The traditional authorship is attributed to the apostle John, identified with the 'lovely disciple', but Tyndale's introduction recognizes that the gospel does not bring explicit proof of authorship and depends on inference from this figure.

Matthew Henry mentions ancient tradition that locates the writing in Ephesus and links the gospel to answers to doctrines that treated Jesus as a mere human being, but this appears as a tradition received, not as independent historical proof.

There is a difference between setting and date of writing: the narrated story occurs in the ministry of Jesus in the 1st century, while the composition is placed at the end of the first century, possibly around AD 90.
The sources describe Ephesus as a context of reception and possible composition, but do not provide a unique and closed chronology.
Some dated elements, such as the government of Caiaphas and Pilate, are presented only when relevant to the narrative and not as a complete period chronology.
The material covers above all John 1, 11 and 21, in addition to the introduction of the gospel; therefore, social and linguistic themes outside these passages appear only when explicitly mentioned.

There are strong confessional readings in the notes, especially about the divinity of Christ, the Holy Spirit, and the mission of the church; this dossier preserves these statements as an interpretation of the sources, without extending them beyond what was said.
dossier.limits: This dossier depends solely on the annexed notes of Tyndale and Matthew Henry and is therefore selective. No external data were used to complete gaps, correct chronologies, or expand beyond what the sources claim. Some information appears as an ancient tradition, editorial inference or theological interpretation, not as a historical certainty demonstrated; this is indicated in each item with explicit-source, interpretation or debated. The coverage is richer for John 1, 11 and 21, because they are the passages provided in detail; other chapters of the gospel only come by abstract in the introduction. There are also controversies about authorship, date and place of composition: the sources mention the apostle John, but recognize that the exact authorship is not explicitly stated in the text and that the date remains approximate. Finally, readings about Judaism, Rome, worship and language are filtered by confessional and pastoral notes, useful for evangelical study, but not equivalent to independent historical proof.
